title: Die zwölf Jäger
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 67. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, gieng/giengen, thut/thats, Rath, Thier, verheirathen, todt, ward).
about: KHM 67, a tale about a promise made at a deathbed and a bride who refuses to be set aside for it. She has eleven maidens found who are her doubles, dresses all twelve in huntsmen’s clothes, and takes service with the king who was once betrothed to her. The two tests that follow — peas strewn on the floor, spinning wheels set in the antechamber — rest on the period’s own certainties about how women walk and what women cannot resist, and the tale takes a quiet pleasure in watching those certainties defeated by twelve women who simply decide not to behave as expected.

sentences.t: Es war einmal ein Königssohn, der hatte eine Braut und hatte sie sehr lieb.
sentences.l: There was once a king’s-son, who had a bride and had her very dear.
sentences.i: There was once a king’s son who had a bride, and he loved her dearly.
sentences.n: “jemanden lieb haben” is the ordinary way of saying one loves a person — lieb held by haben rather than made into a verb, homelier than lieben.

sentences.t: Als er nun bei ihr saß und ganz vergnügt war, da kam die Nachricht daß sein Vater todt krank läge und ihn noch vor seinem Ende zu sehen verlangte.
sentences.l: When he now sat with her and was quite content, there came the news that his father lay deathly ill and desired to see him once more before his end.
sentences.i: Now as he was sitting with her, well content, news came that his father lay mortally ill and desired to see him once more before his end.
sentences.n: “todt krank” = deathly ill (todt is the 1857 spelling of tot). läge is subjunctive: the message is reported, not vouched for by the narrator. verlangte looks like an ordinary past tense but is doing the same reported-speech work — with weak verbs the two forms are identical, and only the context tells you which is meant.

sentences.t: Da sprach er zu seiner Liebsten „ich muß nun fort und muß dich verlassen, da geb ich dir einen Ring zu meinem Andenken.
sentences.l: Then spoke he to his dearest “I must now away and must leave you; so I give you a ring in remembrance of me.
sentences.i: Then he said to his beloved: “Now I must go away and must leave you; so I give you a ring to remember me by.
sentences.n: “zu meinem Andenken” = as a keepsake of me. This ring is the token on which the whole tale finally turns.

sentences.t: Wann ich König bin, komm ich wieder und hol dich heim.“
sentences.l: When I am king, I come again and fetch you home.”
sentences.i: When I am king, I shall come back and fetch you home.”
sentences.n: Wann here is the older spelling and use of wenn, “when”; in modern German wann survives only in questions. “heimholen” = to fetch home, said of bringing a wife home.

sentences.t: Da ritt er fort, und als er bei seinem Vater anlangte, war dieser sterbenskrank und dem Tode nah.
sentences.l: Then he rode away, and when he arrived at his father’s, this one was sick unto death and near to death.
sentences.i: So he rode away; and when he came to his father, the old man was sick unto death and near his end.
sentences.n: anlangen = to arrive, reach a place; modern German kept ankommen and left this one behind. dieser, “this one”, points back to the last person named — the father.

sentences.t: Er sprach zu ihm „liebster Sohn, ich habe dich vor meinem Ende noch einmal sehen wollen, versprich mir nach meinem Willen dich zu verheirathen,“ und nannte ihm eine gewisse Königstochter, die sollte seine Gemahlin werden.
sentences.l: He spoke to him “dearest son, I have wanted to see you once more before my end; promise me to marry according to my will,” and named to him a certain king’s-daughter — she was to become his wife.
sentences.i: He said to him: “Dearest son, I have wished to see you once more before my end; promise me to marry as I would have you marry” — and he named a certain king’s daughter, who was to be his wife.
sentences.n: “sehen wollen” where you would expect gewollt: when a modal governs another verb in the perfect, German puts both in the infinitive (the double infinitive). verheirathen keeps the archaic th of modern verheiraten.

sentences.t: Der Sohn war so betrübt, daß er sich gar nicht bedachte, sondern sprach „ja lieber Vater, was euer Wille ist, soll geschehen,“ und darauf schloß der König die Augen und starb.
sentences.l: The son was so grieved that he did not consider at all, but spoke “yes, dear father, what your will is shall happen,” and thereupon the king closed the eyes and died.
sentences.i: The son was so stricken that he did not stop to think, but said: “Yes, dear father, what you will shall be done” — and thereupon the king closed his eyes and died.
sentences.n: “sich bedenken” = to think a thing over. euer is the respectful plural “your” that a son uses to his father — the same deference faithful Heinrich shows his master in KHM 1.

sentences.t: Als nun der Sohn zum König ausgerufen und die Trauerzeit verflossen war, mußte er das Versprechen halten, das er seinem Vater gegeben hatte, und ließ um die Königstochter werben, und sie ward ihm auch zugesagt.
sentences.l: When now the son had been proclaimed king and the time of mourning had passed away, he had to keep the promise that he had given his father, and had suit made for the king’s-daughter, and she was promised to him too.
sentences.i: Now when the son had been proclaimed king and the time of mourning was over, he had to keep the promise he had given his father; he had suit made for the king’s daughter, and she was duly promised to him.
sentences.n: “um jemanden werben” = to sue for someone’s hand; “ließ… werben” means the suit was made for him by envoys, not in person. verflossen — of time, literally “flowed away”.

sentences.t: Das hörte seine erste Braut und grämte sich über die Untreue so sehr, daß sie fast vergieng.
sentences.l: That heard his first bride, and grieved over the faithlessness so much that she nearly perished.
sentences.i: His first bride heard of it, and grieved so bitterly over his faithlessness that she nearly perished.
sentences.n: vergieng (modern verging), from vergehen: of time it means simply “to pass”, but of a person it means to waste away, to be undone.

sentences.t: Da sprach ihr Vater zu ihr „liebstes Kind, warum bist du so traurig? was du dir wünschest, das sollst du haben.“
sentences.l: Then her father spoke to her “dearest child, why are you so sad? what you wish yourself, that you shall have.”
sentences.i: Then her father said to her: “Dearest child, why are you so sad? Whatever you wish for, you shall have.”
sentences.n: “was du dir wünschest, das sollst du haben” is the old correlative frame: the was-clause first, then das gathering it up. sich etwas wünschen puts the wisher in the dative.

sentences.t: Sie bedachte sich einen Augenblick, dann sprach sie „lieber Vater, ich wünsche mir elf Mädchen, von Angesicht Gestalt und Wuchs mir völlig gleich.“
sentences.l: She considered a moment, then she spoke “dear father, I wish myself eleven girls, in face, figure and build wholly like me.”
sentences.i: She thought for a moment, then said: “Dear father, I wish for eleven maidens exactly like me in face, figure and stature.”
sentences.n: Angesicht is the elevated word for the face, the countenance; Wuchs is one’s growth, one’s build. The 1857 text runs the three nouns together without commas, and we keep its punctuation.

sentences.t: Sprach der König „wenns möglich ist, soll dein Wunsch erfüllt werden,“ und ließ in seinem ganzen Reich so lange suchen, bis elf Jungfrauen gefunden waren, seiner Tochter von Angesicht Gestalt und Wuchs völlig gleich.
sentences.l: Spoke the king “if it is possible, your wish shall be fulfilled,” and had search made in his whole kingdom so long until eleven maidens were found, wholly like his daughter in face, figure and build.
sentences.i: The king said: “If it is possible, your wish shall be granted” — and had search made through his whole kingdom until eleven maidens were found, exactly like his daughter in face, figure and stature.
sentences.n: The sentence opens with its verb — “Sprach der König” rather than “Der König sprach” — a narrative inversion that keeps dialogue moving; it comes back three more times in the exchange with the lion.

sentences.t: Als sie zu der Königstochter kamen, ließ diese zwölf Jägerkleider machen, eins wie das andere, und die elf Jungfrauen mußten die Jägerkleider anziehen, und sie selber zog das zwölfte an.
sentences.l: When they came to the king’s-daughter, this one had twelve huntsmen’s-suits made, one like the other, and the eleven maidens had to put the huntsmen’s clothes on, and she herself put on the twelfth.
sentences.n: “ließ … machen” is causative lassen: she does not make the clothes, she has them made. anziehen is separable, its particle at the end of each clause.

sentences.t: Darauf nahm sie Abschied von ihrem Vater und ritt mit ihnen fort und ritt an den Hof ihres ehemaligen Bräutigams, den sie so sehr liebte.
sentences.l: Thereupon she took leave of her father and rode away with them, and rode to the court of her former bridegroom, whom she loved so much.
sentences.i: Thereupon she took leave of her father and rode away with them, to the court of her former bridegroom, whom she loved so dearly.
sentences.n: A Bräutigam is a man betrothed but not yet married, the counterpart of Braut; both words cover the whole span from the betrothal to the wedding day.

sentences.t: Da fragte sie an ob er Jäger brauchte und ob er sie nicht alle zusammen in seinen Dienst nehmen wollte.
sentences.l: Then she asked whether he needed huntsmen, and whether he would not take them all together into his service.
sentences.n: anfragen (separable) = to make inquiry; the an sits at the end, “fragte sie an”. “in Dienst nehmen” is the ordinary phrase for hiring a retainer.

sentences.t: Der König sah sie an und erkannte sie nicht; weil es aber so schöne Leute waren, sprach er ja, er wollte sie gerne nehmen; und da waren sie die zwölf Jäger des Königs.
sentences.l: The king looked at them and did not recognize them; but because they were such handsome folk, he said yes, he would gladly take them; and so they were the king’s twelve huntsmen.
sentences.i: The king looked at them and did not know her; but because they were such handsome folk, he said yes, he would gladly take them — and so they became the king’s twelve huntsmen.
sentences.n: “erkannte sie nicht”: sie is both “her” and “them”, and German lets the ambiguity stand where English has to choose one.

sentences.t: Der König aber hatte einen Löwen, das war ein wunderliches Thier, denn er wußte alles Verborgene und Heimliche.
sentences.l: The king however had a lion; that was a wondrous beast, for he knew everything hidden and secret.
sentences.i: But the king had a lion, and it was a marvellous beast, for he knew all that was hidden and secret.
sentences.n: wunderlich here means “wondrous, uncanny”; in modern German it has drifted to “odd, peculiar”. “alles Verborgene und Heimliche” — adjectives used as neuter nouns, “everything hidden and secret”. Heimlich still carries its old sense of what is kept close.

sentences.t: Es trug sich zu, daß er eines Abends zum König sprach „du meinst du hättest da zwölf Jäger?“
sentences.l: It came to pass that one evening he spoke to the king “you think you have twelve huntsmen there?”
sentences.i: It came to pass that one evening he said to the king: “You think you have twelve huntsmen there?”
sentences.n: “eines Abends” is a genitive of time, “one evening”. hättest is subjunctive: the lion frames the twelve huntsmen as the king’s belief, not as fact.

sentences.t: „Ja,“ sagte der König, „zwölf Jäger sinds.“
sentences.l: “Yes,” said the king, “twelve huntsmen they are.”

sentences.t: Sprach der Löwe weiter „du irrst dich, das sind zwölf Mädchen.“
sentences.l: Spoke the lion further “you are mistaken, those are twelve girls.”
sentences.i: The lion went on: “You are mistaken — those are twelve maidens.”

sentences.t: Antwortete der König „das ist nimmermehr wahr, wie willst du mir das beweisen?“
sentences.l: Answered the king “that is never true; how will you prove that to me?”
sentences.i: The king answered: “That can never be true. How will you prove it to me?”
sentences.n: nimmermehr is an emphatic old never — not in this world. willst here is not “want” but plain intention: how are you going to prove it.

sentences.t: „O, laß nur Erbsen in dein Vorzimmer streuen,“ antwortete der Löwe, „da wirst dus gleich sehen.
sentences.l: “Oh, just have peas strewn in your antechamber,” answered the lion, “there you will see it at once.
sentences.i: “Oh, just have peas strewn in your antechamber,” answered the lion, “and you will see it at once.
sentences.n: “laß streuen” is the causative lassen again: have someone strew them. dus = du es, as sinds above = sind es. A Vorzimmer is the antechamber a visitor must cross to reach the king.

sentences.t: Männer haben einen festen Tritt, wenn die über Erbsen hingehen, regt sich keine, aber Mädchen, die trippeln und trappeln und schlurfeln, und die Erbsen rollen.“
sentences.l: Men have a firm tread; when they walk over peas, not one stirs; but girls, they trip and tramp and shuffle, and the peas roll.”
sentences.i: Men have a firm tread; when they walk across peas, not one of them stirs. But girls — they trip and patter and shuffle, and the peas roll.”
sentences.n: trippeln, trappeln and schlurfeln are sound-words: small quick steps, heavy clumping, shuffling; schlurfeln is rare even in 1857 (modern schlurfen).

sentences.t: Dem König gefiel der Rath wohl, und er ließ die Erbsen streuen.
sentences.l: The counsel pleased the king well, and he had the peas strewn.
sentences.n: gefallen puts the person pleased in the dative: “dem König gefiel der Rath”. Rath is the 1857 spelling of Rat, counsel — the same word as the Räthe, the councillors.

sentences.t: Es war aber ein Diener des Königs, der war den Jägern gut, und wie er hörte daß sie sollten auf die Probe gestellt werden, gieng er hin und erzählte ihnen alles wieder, und sprach „der Löwe will dem König weis machen ihr wärt Mädchen.“
sentences.l: There was however a servant of the king; that one was well disposed to the huntsmen, and as he heard that they were to be put to the test, he went there and told them everything again, and spoke “the lion wants to make the king believe you were girls.”
sentences.i: But there was a servant of the king who was kindly disposed to the huntsmen; and when he heard that they were to be put to the test, he went and told them the whole of it, saying: “The lion wants to persuade the king that you are maidens.”
sentences.n: “jemandem gut sein” = to be fond of someone, well disposed towards them. “weis machen” (modern weismachen) = to make someone believe what is not so. wärt is subjunctive, marking the lion’s claim as claim.

sentences.t: Da dankte ihm die Königstochter und sprach hernach zu ihren Jungfrauen „thut euch Gewalt an und tretet fest auf die Erbsen.“
sentences.l: Then the king’s-daughter thanked him and spoke afterward to her maidens “do violence to yourselves and tread firmly on the peas.”
sentences.i: Then the king’s daughter thanked him, and afterwards said to her maidens: “Force yourselves, and tread firmly on the peas.”
sentences.n: “sich Gewalt anthun” (modern antun) = to force oneself, to do violence to one’s own nature — the phrase comes back twice more, and it is the tale’s whole method. thut and angethan keep the archaic th of thun, modern tun.

sentences.t: Als nun der König am andern Morgen die zwölf Jäger zu sich rufen ließ, und sie ins Vorzimmer kamen, wo die Erbsen lagen, so traten sie so fest darauf und hatten einen so sichern starken Gang, daß auch nicht eine rollte, oder sich bewegte.
sentences.l: When now the king the next morning had the twelve huntsmen called to him, and they came into the antechamber where the peas lay, they trod so firmly upon them and had so sure and strong a gait that not even one rolled or moved.
sentences.i: Now when the king had the twelve huntsmen called to him the next morning, and they came into the antechamber where the peas lay, they trod so firmly upon them, with so sure and strong a stride, that not a single one rolled or stirred.
sentences.n: darauf = da + auf, standing in for “on them”: German fuses pronoun and preposition when the thing referred to is not a person. “auch nicht eine” = not so much as one.

sentences.t: Da giengen sie wieder fort, und der König sprach zum Löwen „du hast mich belogen, sie gehen ja wie Männer.“
sentences.l: Then they went away again, and the king spoke to the lion “you have lied to me; they walk indeed like men.”
sentences.i: Then they went away again, and the king said to the lion: “You have lied to me — why, they walk like men.”
sentences.n: belügen = to lie to someone, taking a direct object where English needs “to”. ja here is not “yes” but a flavouring particle: “why, …”, “after all”.

sentences.t: Antwortete der Löwe „sie habens gewußt, daß sie sollten auf die Probe gestellt werden, und haben sich Gewalt angethan.
sentences.l: Answered the lion “they knew it, that they were to be put to the test, and have done violence to themselves.
sentences.i: The lion answered: “They knew they were to be put to the test, and forced themselves.
sentences.n: habens is haben es, and the es is a placeholder pointing forward to the daß-clause: they knew it, namely that.

sentences.t: Laß nur einmal zwölf Spinnräder ins Vorzimmer bringen, so werden sie herzukommen und werden sich daran freuen, und das thut kein Mann.“
sentences.l: Just have twelve spinning-wheels brought into the antechamber; then they will come up to them and will take delight in them, and that no man does.”
sentences.i: Just have twelve spinning wheels brought into the antechamber, and they will come up to them and take delight in them — and no man does that.”
sentences.n: The spinning wheel is the emblem of women’s work in these tales, as unmistakable as the huntsman’s coat is of men’s. “sich an etwas freuen” = to take pleasure in something.

sentences.t: Dem König gefiel der Rath, und er ließ die Spinnräder ins Vorzimmer stellen.
sentences.l: The counsel pleased the king, and he had the spinning-wheels set in the antechamber.

sentences.t: Der Diener aber, ders redlich mit den Jägern meinte, gieng hin und entdeckte ihnen den Anschlag.
sentences.l: But the servant, who meant it honestly with the huntsmen, went there and disclosed the plot to them.
sentences.i: But the servant, who meant honestly by the huntsmen, went and disclosed the scheme to them.
sentences.n: ders = der es. “es redlich mit jemandem meinen” = to mean well by someone. entdecken here has its older sense of uncovering, disclosing, rather than discovering.

sentences.t: Da sprach die Königstochter, als sie allein waren, zu ihren elf Mädchen „thut euch Gewalt an und blickt euch nicht um nach den Spinnrädern.“
sentences.l: Then the king’s-daughter spoke, when they were alone, to her eleven girls “do violence to yourselves and do not look round after the spinning-wheels.”
sentences.i: Then, when they were alone, the king’s daughter said to her eleven maidens: “Force yourselves, and do not look round at the spinning wheels.”
sentences.n: “sich umblicken nach” = to look round at something; the reflexive euch and the particle um are both required, the um at the end.

sentences.t: Wie nun der König am andern Morgen seine zwölf Jäger rufen ließ, so kamen sie durch das Vorzimmer und sahen die Spinnräder gar nicht an.
sentences.l: When now the king the next morning had his twelve huntsmen called, they came through the antechamber and did not look at the spinning-wheels at all.
sentences.i: Now when the king had his twelve huntsmen called the next morning, they came through the antechamber and never so much as glanced at the spinning wheels.

sentences.t: Da sprach der König wiederum zum Löwen „du hast mich belogen, es sind Männer, denn sie haben die Spinnräder nicht angesehen.“
sentences.l: Then the king spoke to the lion again “you have lied to me; they are men, for they have not looked at the spinning-wheels.”
sentences.i: Then the king said to the lion again: “You have lied to me. They are men, for they never looked at the spinning wheels.”

sentences.t: Der Löwe antwortete „sie habens gewußt, daß sie sollten auf die Probe gestellt werden, und haben sich Gewalt angethan.“
sentences.l: The lion answered “they knew it, that they were to be put to the test, and have done violence to themselves.”
sentences.i: The lion answered: “They knew they were to be put to the test, and forced themselves.”
sentences.n: Word for word the answer he gave after the peas. The tale lets him be right twice and be disbelieved twice.

sentences.t: Der König aber wollte dem Löwen nicht mehr glauben.
sentences.l: The king however would believe the lion no more.

sentences.t: Die zwölf Jäger folgten dem König beständig zur Jagd, und er hatte sie je länger je lieber.
sentences.l: The twelve huntsmen followed the king constantly to the hunt, and he had them the longer the dearer.
sentences.i: The twelve huntsmen went with the king constantly to the hunt, and the longer it went on the fonder he grew of them.
sentences.n: “je länger je lieber” = the longer, the dearer — a set comparative pattern; modern German would say “je länger, desto lieber”.

sentences.t: Nun geschah es, daß, als sie einmal auf der Jagd waren, Nachricht kam, die Braut des Königs wäre im Anzug.
sentences.l: Now it happened that, when they were once at the hunt, news came that the king’s bride was on the way.
sentences.i: Now it came to pass that once, while they were at the hunt, word came that the king’s bride was approaching.
sentences.n: “im Anzug sein” = to be approaching, drawing near — said of an army, a storm or, as here, a bride; it has nothing to do with the modern Anzug, a suit of clothes. wäre is again reported speech.

sentences.t: Wie die rechte Braut das hörte, thats ihr so weh, daß es ihr fast das Herz abstieß, und sie ohnmächtig auf die Erde fiel.
sentences.l: When the right bride heard that, it hurt her so that it nearly struck the heart from her, and she fell fainting to the earth.
sentences.i: When the true bride heard it, it pained her so that it all but broke her heart, and she fell to the ground in a faint.
sentences.n: rechte here is “true, rightful”, not “right-hand”. thats = that es, with the archaic that for tat. “das Herz abstoßen” is a rare old idiom for what English calls a heart breaking; the image seems to be of the heart struck from its place, though its exact force is hard to pin down.

sentences.t: Der König meinte seinem lieben Jäger sei etwas begegnet, lief hinzu und wollte ihm helfen, und zog ihm den Handschuh aus.
sentences.l: The king thought something had befallen his dear huntsman, ran up and wanted to help him, and pulled the glove off him.
sentences.i: The king thought something had befallen his dear huntsman, ran up to help him, and pulled off his glove.
sentences.n: begegnen takes the dative — the thing befalls to him; sei is the reported-speech subjunctive carrying the king’s supposition. “zog ihm den Handschuh aus” — the dative ihm marks whose glove it is, where English simply says “his”.

sentences.t: Da erblickte er den Ring, den er seiner ersten Braut gegeben, und als er ihr in das Gesicht sah, erkannte er sie.
sentences.l: Then he caught sight of the ring that he had given his first bride, and when he looked her in the face, he recognized her.
sentences.i: Then he caught sight of the ring he had given his first bride; and when he looked into her face, he knew her.
sentences.n: gegeben stands without its auxiliary hatte — Grimm often drops the auxiliary in a relative clause. “ihr in das Gesicht sah” again puts the person in the dative: looked, to her, into the face.

sentences.t: Da ward sein Herz so gerührt, daß er sie küßte, und als sie die Augen aufschlug, sprach er „du bist mein und ich bin dein, und kein Mensch auf der Welt kann das ändern.“
sentences.l: Then his heart became so moved that he kissed her, and when she opened the eyes, he spoke “you are mine and I am yours, and no person in the world can change that.”
sentences.i: Then his heart was so moved that he kissed her; and when she opened her eyes, he said: “You are mine and I am yours, and no one in the world can alter it.”
sentences.n: “du bist mein und ich bin dein” is an old betrothal formula, known in German love-poetry for centuries before the Grimms; set here, it is the tale’s true wedding vow. “die Augen aufschlagen” = to open one’s eyes, literally to strike them open.

sentences.t: Zu der andern Braut aber schickte er einen Boten, und ließ sie bitten in ihr Reich zurückzukehren, denn er habe schon eine Gemahlin, und wer einen alten Schlüssel wiedergefunden habe, brauche den neuen nicht.
sentences.l: But to the other bride he sent a messenger, and had her asked to return into her kingdom, for he had a wife already, and whoever had found an old key again did not need the new one.
sentences.i: But to the other bride he sent a messenger, asking her to return to her own kingdom, for he had a wife already; and whoever has found an old key again has no need of the new one.
sentences.n: habe and brauche are subjunctives carrying the message’s own words: everything after denn is the king’s, not the narrator’s. The proverb of the two keys is all the judgment the tale passes on the deathbed promise.

sentences.t: Darauf ward die Hochzeit gefeiert, und der Löwe kam wieder in Gnade, weil er doch die Wahrheit gesagt hatte.
sentences.l: Thereupon the wedding was celebrated, and the lion came into favour again, because he had after all told the truth.
sentences.i: Thereupon the wedding was celebrated, and the lion came back into favour, for he had told the truth after all.
sentences.n: “in Gnade kommen” = to be restored to favour. doch here is not “but” but a small concessive particle — he had told the truth after all.
